q: How do you say the Spanish vowel in no?
o: Short and pure, with no glide at the end
Like the o in English go, ending in a w
Like the a in English about
It is silent at the end of a word
why: Spanish vowels are short and pure: the o never slides into a w.

q: Why does adiós have an accent mark?
o: Every word ending in s needs one
It shows that the o is long
Without it, the stress would fall on the first syllable
It turns the word into a question
why: adiós ends in s, so the rule would stress the next-to-last syllable; the accent mark moves the stress to the end.

q: How is the j pronounced in el jugo (the juice)?
o: Like the j in English juice
Like the y in English yes
A breathy h, like a sigh
why: j is always a breathy h sound in Spanish, never the English j.

q: You meet your coworker's grandfather for the first time. What do you ask?
why: An older person you don't know gets usted: ¿Cómo está usted?

q: Why is it buenos días but buenas noches?
o: días is masculine and noches is feminine, and the word for good matches each
No reason: either form works with either word
why: bueno agrees with the noun: días is masculine, noches is feminine.

q: How do you say My name is Carlos?
why: me llamo already means my name is; it needs no es, and the small word is me, not mi.

q: Which is correct?
why: día ends in -a but is masculine: el día.

q: Two boys and one girl are together. Which do you use for the group?
o: las niñas, because the girl decides
los niños, because a mixed group takes the masculine plural
why: A mixed group takes the masculine plural: los niños.

q: How do you make la ciudad plural?
why: ciudad ends in a consonant, so it adds -es, and la becomes las.

q: How do you say I like chicken (pollo)?
why: Things in general keep the article in Spanish, and pollo is masculine: el pollo.

q: Why is it el agua, if agua is feminine?
o: A feminine noun that starts with a stressed a takes el in the singular
why: el agua avoids two a sounds in a row; the noun stays feminine.

q: What does unas tortillas mean?
why: unos and unas mean some or a few.

q: A man says I'm a nurse. Which is right?
why: No article before a job, and a man is enfermero.

q: Which form of ser goes with usted?
why: usted takes the same form as él: es.

q: Why can you say Soy de Chicago without yo?
o: soy already shows that the subject is yo
yo is only used with usted
It is a mistake, but people understand it
why: The verb ending tells you who: soy can only mean I am.

q: Where does a color usually go?
o: Before the noun, as in English
At the end of the sentence
why: Spanish puts the adjective after the noun: la camisa roja.

q: the white shirts =
why: Feminine plural noun, feminine plural adjective, after the noun: las camisas blancas.

q: Which adjective has the same form with el and la?
why: Adjectives ending in -e do not change for gender: el suéter verde, la falda verde.

q: Where is the museum? =
why: Where something is: estar, and one museum takes está.

q: Which form of estar goes with ustedes?
why: ustedes takes the same form as ellos: están.

q: Why is it Monterrey está en México, though the city never moves?
o: estar is for where something is, whether it can move or not
It's a mistake; it should be es
why: Location uses estar, permanent or not.

q: Which is the best rule of thumb?
o: ser for permanent things, estar for temporary ones
ser for what something is; estar for where it is and how it is right now
estar for people, ser for things
ser in questions, estar in answers
why: What something is takes ser; where it is and how it is right now take estar.

q: The party is at the hotel. =
why: Where an event takes place uses ser: La fiesta es en el hotel.

q: What does Carlos es aburrido mean?
why: ser aburrido is boring; estar aburrido is bored.

q: There are three bedrooms. =
why: hay means both there is and there are, and it never changes.

q: Which is correct?
why: hay introduces something new, so it takes un, not el.

q: Your friend knows the café you mean. How do you tell her where it is?
why: A particular thing you both know: estar says where it is.

q: Complete 'We live in Miami': Nosotros ___ en Miami.
why: -ir verbs end in -imos in the nosotros form.

q: You ask a stranger if they speak English. Which is right?
why: Usted takes the él form: habla.

q: How do you say 'I'm studying Spanish' (this year, at school)?
why: The simple present covers 'I'm studying' for things going on these days.

q: 'Do you speak English?' (to a friend) =
why: No do in Spanish: the tú form hablas plus a rising voice makes the question.

q: 'How many hours do you work?' Which is right?
why: Cuántas agrees with horas, which is feminine plural.

q: 'Where does Ana live?' =
why: Question word, then the verb, then the subject; one person takes vive.

q: 'It's three o'clock' =
why: Three is plural, so son, with las for the hours.

q: How do you write 120?
why: Before another number, cien becomes ciento, and no y follows it.

q: 'How much are the shoes?' =
why: Los zapatos is plural, so the verb is cuestan.

q: 'his books' =
why: The possessive agrees with libros, which is plural: sus.

q: 'this shirt' =
why: Camisa is feminine, so esta. Está with an accent mark means is.

q: 'Our grandmother lives in Cancún' =
why: Nuestra agrees with abuela: feminine singular.

q: 'I'm 25 years old' =
why: Age uses tener, and the yo form is tengo.

q: 'It's cold today' (the weather) =
why: Weather uses hacer. Tengo frío is about your body.

q: 'They go to school' =
why: The ellos form of ir is van.

q: 'We can' =
why: The nosotros form keeps the stem of the infinitive: pod-.

q: You ask a stranger: 'Can you help me?'
why: To a stranger, use the usted form puede.

q: 'I ask for help' =
why: To ask for something, use pedir: pido.

q: 'I like pizza' =
why: The pizza is the subject: me gusta la pizza.

q: 'I like tacos' =
why: Gustan agrees with los tacos, and the article stays.

q: 'We like to dance' =
why: An activity takes gusta, and nos shows who likes it.

q: 'I get up at seven' =
why: Yo takes me and the ending -o.

q: 'What's your name?' (to a friend) =
why: Tú takes te and the ending -s.

q: 'We go to bed at eleven' =
why: Nosotros takes nos, and the nosotros form keeps the o.

q: 'I see Ana' =
why: A person who receives the action takes the personal a.

q: 'Ana's car' =
why: Spanish has no 's: el carro de Ana.

q: 'Thanks for everything' =
why: Thanks always take por.

q: How do you say "It's very cold" about the weather?
why: Weather uses hacer + a noun, and a noun takes mucho, not muy.

q: Which word completes "Tengo ___ sed" (I'm very thirsty)?
why: sed is a feminine noun, so it takes mucha.

q: "You speak very well" is…
why: bien is a describing word, so muy goes right before it.

q: Which word means "because"?
why: porque, one word with no accent mark, means because. ¿Por qué? asks why.

q: How do you write "Sofía and Isabel"?
why: Isabel starts with an ee sound, so y becomes e.

q: Your friend says "No me gusta el frío." You don't like it either. You say…
why: tampoco agrees with a no; también agrees with a yes.

q: "On the right" is…
why: derecha (with -a) is right, and it takes a la.

q: A stranger tells you "Siga derecho." What do you do?
why: siga = keep going, derecho = straight ahead.

q: "next to the bank" is…
why: a + el becomes al, and de + el becomes del.

q: "I'm going to eat" is…
why: ir + a + infinitive: voy a comer. The a is never dropped.

q: Which form goes with nosotros?
why: nosotros takes vamos: vamos a viajar.

q: "Are you going to travel on Saturday?" (to a friend)
why: vas for tú, then a + infinitive; days take el, not en.

q: "¿La camisa? ___ compro." Which word fits?
why: camisa is feminine and singular, so la.

q: "I call her" (Ana) is…
why: The pronoun la goes before the verb; ella is never used for her after a verb.

q: Which pair both mean "I'm going to buy them" (los zapatos)?
why: los goes before voy or is attached to comprar; zapatos is masculine, so los.

q: "She spoke" is…
why: habló, with the accent on the end, is the él/ella form of the preterite. hablo means I speak.

q: "I went to the movies" is…
why: fui is the yo form of ir in the preterite, written with no accent mark.

q: Your Mexican friend asks "¿Ya comiste?" She means…
why: Latin America uses ya + preterite for have you… yet.

q: A sign says "Se habla español." It means…
why: Impersonal se: no person is named, so it means Spanish is spoken.

q: "Houses for sale" on a sign is…
why: casas is plural, so standard written Spanish makes the verb plural too: se venden.

q: "How do you say this in Spanish?" (asking in general) is…
why: se + the él form of decir: se dice.

q: A Dominican friend says "¿Cómo tú 'tá?" (written ¿Cómo tú estás?). She means…
why: It's ¿Cómo estás? with tú before the verb and the s softened.

q: In Santo Domingo you hear "polque". Which word is it?
why: r at the end of a syllable can sound like l: porque.

q: What is a guagua?
why: Regional (Caribbean): la guagua is the bus.
